prompt: Walk me through your resume.
variants: Take me through your work history.
Talk me through your background, starting wherever you like.
intent: Checks that you can tell your history as a coherent story with a direction, not a list of dates.
answerGuide: Begin with the most recent role and what you owned.
Move backward through one or two earlier steps, naming the skill each added.
End on why the thread leads to this role.
Keep to two or three minutes.
pitfalls: Spending half the time on the oldest job.
followUps: Which role did you enjoy most, and why?
How did one role lead to the next?

prompt: Your degree is in a different field. Why are you applying for this kind of role?
variants: How does your education relate to this job?
Why science if you want to work in software or operations?
intent: Probes whether the degree mismatch is a real commitment issue or a story you can explain with transferable skills.
answerGuide: Acknowledge the mismatch briefly and without apology.
Name two transferable strengths from the degree: rigor, working with data, precision, learning technical material.
Point to work experience that proves the new direction is real.
State why you chose this path.
pitfalls: Sounding like the degree was a mistake.
Not linking to evidence of the new direction.
followUps: Did you ever want to work in your degree field?
What would you say to someone who thinks you lack the right background?
Which course helped you most for this?

prompt: I see a gap on your resume. What were you doing?
variants: Can you explain the time between jobs?
What have you been doing since your last role?
intent: Looks for a straightforward, undefensive explanation and evidence you stayed active.
answerGuide: Say plainly what the gap was (one sentence, truthful).
Name what you did that is relevant: learning, projects, freelance, certifications.
Close on readiness and enthusiasm for starting now.
pitfalls: Vague answers that make it sound worse.
followUps: Why did it take that long?
Are you ready to start immediately?

prompt: You were in your last role for less than two years, and your earlier role was short too. Why?
variants: Why have your jobs been short?
Are you a job hopper?
intent: Checks stability concerns and whether you understand the pattern.
answerGuide: Give honest reasons for each move without blame (contract end, scope, company change).
Show what you gained in each.
Reassure with a reason this role is a stable fit.
followUps: How long do you want to stay?
What did you learn from the shortest job?

prompt: Why did you move from customer support into project or product work, and why do you want to move again?
variants: Explain the progression in your career.
Why the change from your earlier job type?
intent: Looks at the logic of your moves and whether you are chasing direction or novelty.
answerGuide: Link each step: what you outgrew and what you wanted next.
Name the skill continuity (customer problems, requirements, quality).
State why the next step is a natural continuation.
followUps: What did you miss from the earlier role?
What was the real reason for the switch?

prompt: Tell me about a role on your resume in more detail: what did your day look like?
variants: What did a typical week involve?
Describe your responsibilities there.
intent: Confirms the resume is accurate and shows how deep your experience really is.
answerGuide: Describe a typical week with real tasks and proportions.
Name tools and who you worked with.
Add one result you are proud of.
followUps: Which tool did you use most?
What would your manager say you owned?

prompt: Tell me about a resume bullet: how did you get that result?
variants: You list an improvement in a metric. What exactly did you do?
How did you measure that number?
intent: Verifies claims; interviewers often pick one number and dig.
answerGuide: Start with the baseline and how it was measured.
Describe your specific actions in order.
Explain what else may have contributed, honestly.

prompt: How would you rate your SQL skills, and what have you actually done with them?
variants: How comfortable are you with SQL?
Describe your experience querying data.
intent: Checks honest calibration of a self-taught skill against real use.
answerGuide: State your level plainly: strong on retrieval and reporting, not database design or administration.
Give two real examples of queries or reports and what they answered.
Say what you do not know yet and are learning.
pitfalls: Being unable to describe a real query.
followUps: Write or describe a query joining two tables.
What is the difference between WHERE and HAVING?
How do you check a query result is right?

prompt: What tools and software have you used, and at what level?
variants: What is your tech stack experience?
Which tools are you strongest in?
intent: Quickly maps your toolset and checks honesty about depth.
answerGuide: Group tools by daily use, occasional use and learning.
Give one concrete task for each daily tool.
Flag what you are new to without overclaiming.
followUps: Which would you trust yourself to teach?
Which have you not used on the job?
How quickly could you learn ours?

prompt: What are your salary expectations?
variants: What salary range are you looking for?
What compensation do you need?
intent: Screens for budget fit and negotiating maturity.
answerGuide: Give a researched range based on market data for role, level and location, or ask for their range first.
Say you are flexible based on the whole package.
Keep it brief and confident.
pitfalls: Naming a number too low out of nerves.
followUps: How did you arrive at that range?
What if our range is lower?

prompt: What did you earn in your last role?
variants: What is your current salary?
intent: Some recruiters ask; checks how you handle a question that may be restricted by law in some places.
answerGuide: Redirect to what you expect for this role and level using market data you researched.
If the law in your state bars the question, say you would rather focus on this role's range; otherwise answer honestly.
Stay polite and do not inflate.

prompt: Are you comfortable working remotely full time? What is your setup?
variants: Do you have a suitable home office?
How do you manage remote work day to day?
intent: Practical readiness: equipment, connection, workspace, hours.
answerGuide: Describe a dedicated workspace, reliable internet and a backup.
Mention routines that keep you reachable and productive.
Show prior remote or independent experience.
followUps: What if your internet goes down?
How do you separate work and home?

prompt: This role is remote with some team hours that may not match yours. Is that workable?
variants: Are you available during our core hours?
Can you work across time zones?
intent: Checks whether your available hours overlap the team's core hours and whether you ask about them instead of assuming.
answerGuide: Give your time zone and the hours you can reliably work, with the overlap this team needs.
Say what flexibility you can offer (early starts, an occasional late meeting).
Ask what the core hours are so you are not guessing.
followUps: How do you handle urgent evening requests?

prompt: When could you start, and are you interviewing elsewhere?
variants: What is your timeline?
Where are you in your job search?
intent: Logistics and competition check; recruiters use it to schedule.
answerGuide: Give a real start date including any notice you owe.
Say you are talking to a few similar teams without naming them.
State that this role is a priority and what would accelerate your decision.
followUps: What would you need to decide?

prompt: Do you have any commitments that would affect working this schedule or location?
variants: Are you authorized to work here and available for the hours listed?
intent: A logistics screen for hours, location and commitments; the interviewer wants a clear yes or no on the schedule, not personal detail.
answerGuide: Say yes or no to the stated schedule and location in one sentence.
Mention fixed constraints (a regular appointment, a time zone) only as availability facts, not reasons.
Offer the hours you can reliably work and ask about core hours.
followUps: Anything we should know to plan?
Are you able to start on a fixed date?

prompt: How would you describe your experience with Agile, Scrum or Kanban?
variants: Have you worked in an agile team?
What agile ceremonies have you run?
intent: Verifies practical experience rather than textbook knowledge.
answerGuide: Say what you actually ran or took part in: planning, standups, retrospectives, backlog.
Give an example of a retrospective outcome.
Be clear about formal titles or certifications you do not hold.
followUps: What was a retrospective action that stuck?

prompt: What is your experience with test automation or coding?
variants: Can you write automated tests?
How technical are you?
intent: Calibrates your automation level honestly: mostly manual QA with basic Playwright tests you built and ran in a pipeline.
answerGuide: State clearly: mostly manual testing; basic automation learned independently.
Describe what you built and ran, and its limits.
Say what you would learn next.
followUps: How does it run in a pipeline?

prompt: Why did you leave your earlier support job after such a short time, or why did you move on from it?
variants: What happened with the position before your last one?
intent: Probes why an earlier support job was short; a calm, neutral reason and a link to later growth settle it.
answerGuide: Give one neutral true reason (contract or study) in a sentence.
Name what you took from it: case logging in Salesforce and plain-language customer help.
Connect it to the stable, nearly two-year run that followed.
followUps: Who can speak to your work?

prompt: Do you have any questions about your resume that I should clear up, or anything that might concern us?
variants: Is there anything in your background you want to address?
intent: Invites proactive disclosure; shows confidence.
answerGuide: Address the most likely concern head-on (a small-company title, a gap, a different degree).
Reframe with one proof point such as the documentation project and its measured result.
Stop and invite the next question.
followUps: How would you convince a skeptic?
What proof would you point to?

prompt: Can you provide references from recent roles?
variants: Who would speak to your work?
intent: Checks that you have usable references from recent roles who know to expect contact and can speak to specific work.
answerGuide: Name who you would use (a manager, a customer or a colleague) and confirm they know to expect a call.
Say what each can speak to, such as release testing or the documentation rewrite.
Offer contact details when asked.

prompt: Would you accept a contract position or a lower starting salary with a path to raise?
variants: Are you open to contract-to-hire?
intent: Tests flexibility on contract or lower starting pay with a path to raise, and whether you ask about duration, conversion and benefits first.
answerGuide: Say whether you are open to it and what you need to know first: contract length, conversion terms, benefits, hours.
Ask what the path to a raise looks like and when it is reviewed.
Do not agree before seeing the terms in writing.

prompt: Tell me about your education and what you got from it that applies here.
variants: How did your studies prepare you for this?
What courses were relevant?
intent: Looks for a short, confident link from your health science degrees to skills you use at work, with a real example.
answerGuide: Give the two degrees in one sentence with the strongest result.
Pick two transferable skills: analysing data and learning dense material.
Add one work example, such as using health knowledge on a pharmacy staffing product.
followUps: Which course taught you the most?
How do you use it now?

prompt: Your title was Project Manager but your work covered QA, support, documentation and product work. Which job do you actually want?
variants: How do I place you if your title does not match the work?
intent: Resolves the generalist-title worry directly: you must show the pieces, choose an honest focus for this role, and not look scattered.
answerGuide: Say briefly why the title was broad: a small team where one person covered these functions.
Name the strongest strand for this role (for example QA and UAT for a QA analyst) and give one proof point.
Show the connecting thread: knowing how the product is used, tested and supported.
State your preference now and why.
followUps: How would you split your time?
Would you want the other work too?

prompt: Much of what you list is self-taught. How can I trust the level?
variants: How do I verify skills with no certificate?
intent: Tests whether you can offer proof and honest levels: examples, a demonstration, or a practice task.
answerGuide: Say how you learned each skill and where you applied it on the job.
State levels precisely: SQL intermediate for retrieval and reporting, Excel moderate, Playwright basic.
Offer evidence: a query you can explain, a test you ran in a pipeline, a live exercise right now.
Be open about any gaps.
followUps: What would be a quick test?

prompt: Pick any number on your resume and explain exactly how you know it is true.
variants: How was that number calculated?
intent: A resume-probing technique used to catch inflated numbers; the answer shows baseline, method and limits.
answerGuide: Choose your strongest number (ticket inflow down 35 percent) and state baseline, period and source.
Describe how you counted and what you excluded.
State what else could have contributed.
Say what you would measure differently.
followUps: Which of your numbers is weakest?

prompt: Your first support job was short. What happened?
variants: Why did you leave that support role so soon?
intent: Checks you can explain a short tenure in one neutral sentence and show what it led to.
answerGuide: Give the real reason in one sentence (contract or seasonal role, or a decision to return to study) without blame.
Name what you took from it: case documentation in Salesforce, communication with customers.
Connect to what you did next.
Add why your recent role shows stability: nearly two years.

prompt: Your degrees are in health sciences. Why should a software team hire you?
variants: How does biomedical science connect to software work?
intent: Turns a degree mismatch into evidence: learning ability, scientific method and domain knowledge for healthcare software.
answerGuide: Link the degrees to transferable skills: analysing data, careful documentation, learning dense material.
Link to domain: you understand pharmacy and healthcare staffing, which helps in a healthcare-related product.
Show the bridge: the roles and self-study that moved you into software.
Mention strong grades briefly without leaning on them.
pitfalls: Claiming it as a technical qualification.
followUps: What do you still need to learn?

prompt: There is a gap between your 2021 support job and your 2025 project role. What were you doing?
variants: Can you explain the gap on your resume?
intent: A gap question: honest, brief answer in one or two sentences, and the evidence of continued growth.
answerGuide: State the real reason (study, completing degrees) in a factual sentence.
Name what you gained during that time: the degrees and any work or projects.
Move to what you did when you came back to work.
Do not apologise or invent activity.
followUps: Did you work during that time?

prompt: Why are you leaving your current small company?
variants: Why did you leave your last job?
intent: Checks the reason for the move and whether it points forward, since it was a role you held for about 21 months.
answerGuide: State the real reason briefly, framed positively (the scope reached its natural end, looking for a more structured team).
Say what you did there that you are proud of.
Say what you want next that this role offers.
No criticism of the company.
followUps: Did you try to change the role?
What will you not accept in the next one?

prompt: You are early career and light on formal experience. Why should we believe you can do this job?
variants: How do you compare to candidates with more years?
intent: Asked of recent graduates and career changers; looks for proof of capability over years.
answerGuide: Acknowledge your experience honestly: under two years in a software role plus earlier support work.
Give three concrete proofs: UAT and release testing, backlog ownership, and the documentation project with a measured result.
Show learning speed: skills taught yourself.
Say how you would ramp up in the first weeks.
followUps: What would take longest to learn?
What do you expect from your first month?

prompt: A recruiter asks for your salary expectation on the first call. Give me your answer.
variants: What salary range are you looking for?
intent: Practice for the recruiter screen: a researched range, flexibility, and not naming a number before you know the role.
answerGuide: Say you have researched the market for this role, level and location and give a range based on that research.
If the posting has a range, anchor to it; if not, ask for their range first.
Say you are open to discussing the full package once you understand the role.
Do not share past salary if the law or your comfort says otherwise.
pitfalls: Naming a number far below the market.
followUps: What if the range is below yours?

prompt: If we cannot meet your number, what would make the offer work?
variants: How flexible are you on compensation?
intent: A negotiation follow-up: priorities and creative trade-offs.
answerGuide: Say what matters most (base, review date, remote setup, development budget).
Ask what flexibility exists and propose a concrete alternative such as a review at six months.
Stay positive and decisive; do not accept or reject on the spot.
Ask for the offer in writing.

prompt: Are you authorised to work in this country, and what would your start date be?
variants: Do you need sponsorship?
intent: A basic eligibility question every recruiter screen asks; clear and short answers.
answerGuide: Answer the authorization question directly.
Give a realistic start date, including any notice period.
Mention flexibility within reason.
Keep it short.
followUps: Is there anything affecting your start?

prompt: Describe your remote working setup and hours. What time zone will you work in?
variants: Are you set up to work remotely full time?
intent: Practical remote readiness: workspace, connectivity, hours overlap and equipment.
answerGuide: State your location and hours, and how much overlap you can offer.
Describe the workspace, internet and backup (mobile hotspot).
Mention security basics: a private space, locked screen, work device rules.
Offer flexibility on core hours.
followUps: Are you able to travel for onboarding?
How do you separate work and home?

prompt: Pick one job on your resume and walk me through a typical week.
variants: What did you actually do all day at your last company?
intent: A drill-down to test authenticity: specific tasks, tools and proportions.
answerGuide: Describe the week by day with tasks and proportions: sprint events, tickets, UAT, documentation, customer calls.
Name tools used each day (Azure DevOps, Jira, SQL).
Include one challenge and how you handled it.
Be consistent with the resume.
followUps: What was the least favourite part?

prompt: Rate yourself from one to five on SQL, Excel, Jira, Azure DevOps, Playwright and Power BI.
variants: How would you rate your technical skills?
intent: Tests calibrated self-assessment and a refusal to overclaim.
answerGuide: Give honest ratings with a one-line example: SQL intermediate for retrieval and reporting, Excel moderate with pivots and VLOOKUP, daily Jira and Azure DevOps use, basic Playwright, Power BI being learned.
Say where each limit is.
Offer a quick demonstration.
Note what you are improving.
followUps: What would a five look like?

prompt: An interviewer asks, 'Do you plan to have children soon?' How do you respond?
variants: What do you do if the interviewer asks about marital status or family?
intent: Practice for inappropriate questions: stay composed, steer to the job requirement and know your options.
answerGuide: Recognise that personal family plans are not a job requirement and that you are not obliged to answer.
Respond politely by redirecting to the actual concern: availability for the schedule, with a clear answer.
Optionally ask how the question relates to the role.
If it continues or feels discriminatory, end politely and report to the recruiter or HR later.
followUps: What if you want the job?

prompt: An interviewer asks how old you are, where you were born, or whether you have any health conditions. What do you do?
variants: How do you handle questions about age, origin or health?
intent: Covers the other common inappropriate topics and the legitimate versions an employer may ask.
answerGuide: Know the legitimate versions: whether you are authorised to work, whether you can meet the schedule, whether you can perform the essential duties with or without accommodation.
Answer the legitimate version and gently decline the personal detail.
Stay calm and professional.
Note the question and, if concerned, talk to HR or seek advice.
followUps: What if you are asked about accommodations?

prompt: Recruiter screen: in two minutes, who are you, what do you do and what are you looking for?
variants: Give me your 60-second pitch.
intent: A phone-screen opener where a recruiter judges fit against a posting; short, targeted and ending on the role.
answerGuide: Present: what you do now in a sentence.
Past: two or three results that match the posting.
Future: the kind of role you want and why this one.
Under two minutes, plain language.
followUps: What are you not looking for?

prompt: If you joined us, what would your first 90 days look like?
variants: What would you do in your first three months?
intent: A hiring-manager question about realistic ramp-up and your ability to plan without knowing the details.
answerGuide: Month one: learn the product, customers, tools and people; do small tasks.
Month two: own a defined piece of work and share early.
Month three: show a measurable result and propose an improvement.
Add that you would ask what success looks like.
pitfalls: A plan with no learning phase.
followUps: How would you measure your success?

prompt: In a panel, three people ask questions at once and one seems unfriendly. How do you handle it?
variants: How do you perform in a panel interview?
intent: Practical panel round skills: address everyone, answer in order and stay composed.
answerGuide: Take a breath, answer the question as asked, and look at the asker and then others.
If several questions come at once, note them and answer in order or ask which first.
Engage the quiet or sceptical person too without playing to them.
Keep answers shorter than in a one-on-one.
followUps: What if you forget a question?
How do you read the room?

prompt: In a values interview: what is something you would refuse to do at work, even if asked?
variants: Where is your line?
intent: Tests integrity and its practical expression: specific refusals with an alternative offered.
answerGuide: Name a concrete line: falsifying test results, sharing customer data improperly, hiding a known problem.
Show how you would act: refuse, offer a legitimate alternative, escalate if needed.
Mention an example if you have one.
Avoid sounding rigid on matters of preference.
followUps: What would you do if your manager insisted?

prompt: You studied health sciences and now work in software. Are you sure you want to stay in tech?
variants: Will you go back to healthcare?
intent: Tests commitment after a pivot and honest reasons.
answerGuide: Explain the pivot honestly: what drew you to software work and what you found.
Show evidence of staying: skills built and more planned.
Show how health knowledge feeds your work.
Express what you want long term.
followUps: What if you got a clinical offer?

prompt: We run background and reference checks. Is there anything I should know before we do?
variants: Will your references confirm your resume?
intent: A candid-disclosure test: no surprises, with confidence if everything is clean.
answerGuide: Say that everything on the resume is accurate and give any factual note you should flag, such as a title that differs from the work.
Say who your references are and that they know to expect contact.
Offer documentation if needed.
Keep it short.
pitfalls: Waiting for them to find a discrepancy.
followUps: Which job title matches HR records?
Can we contact your current employer?

prompt: How do you use AI tools in your daily work, and would you follow our restrictions on them?
variants: What is your policy on AI at work?
intent: Screens AI judgment: practical productivity use with respect for data policy.
answerGuide: Name a few uses (drafting, summarising notes, explaining errors, generating test ideas) and say you always review the output.
State what you keep out: customer, patient and company-confidential data unless the tool is approved.
Say you follow the employer's policy and ask when it is unclear.
Mention you own the result.
followUps: Which task would you never give it?

prompt: Would you consider a contract-to-hire or a part-time start?
variants: How flexible are you on the type of employment?
intent: Practical flexibility screen: terms, conversion and fit with your needs.
answerGuide: State honestly what you can accept.
Ask about conversion terms, duration, benefits, hours, and pay rate.
Express interest in the work first.
Avoid committing before seeing terms.
followUps: How would you view the risk?
